trivia_fact: Nagios was originally called "NetSaint" when Ethan Galstad created it in 1999. He was forced to rename it in 2002 due to trademark issues with a company that owned "Saint." "Nagios" is a recursive acronym for "Nagios Ain't Gonna Insist On Sainthood."

Prometheus is named after the Greek Titan who stole fire from the gods and gave it to humanity. The metaphor: monitoring gives teams visibility (fire/light) into their systems that would otherwise be hidden.

Prometheus was created at SoundCloud in 2012 by ex-Google engineers Matt T. Proud and Julius Volz. They were inspired by Google's internal monitoring system Borgmon, which monitored the Borg cluster manager.

Grafana's name is often said to be a portmanteau of "graph" and "Kibana," but creator Torkel Odegaard has said he simply liked how it sounded. The word evokes "graphing" and the suffix gives it a tool-like feel.

Google's SRE book defines four golden signals for monitoring any system: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation. These four metrics are considered the minimum viable set for understanding service health.

Brendan Gregg created the USE method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) for analyzing system performance. It focuses on hardware resources rather than application metrics, making it complementary to RED.
Tom Wilkie created the RED method (Rate, Errors, Duration) at Weaveworks for monitoring request-driven microservices. It maps directly to the end-user experience and pairs naturally with Prometheus.

Zabbix founder Alexei Vladishev chose the name simply because he liked how it sounded. It has no acronym, no meaning, and no hidden etymology — he just wanted a unique, memorable name that started with a letter near the end of the alphabet.

Averages are misleading for latency: if 99 requests take 1ms and one takes 10 seconds, the average is ~101ms — masking the outlier. The p99 (10s) reveals the pain that real users feel. Gil Tene's "How NOT to Measure Latency" popularized this insight.

Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) was published as RFC 1067 in 1988, making it older than HTTP, Linux, and most engineers working with it today. SNMPv3 (1998) finally added encryption, a decade later.

Nagios popularized the concept of check plugins with a simple contract: exit code 0=OK, 1=WARNING, 2=CRITICAL, 3=UNKNOWN. This convention became an informal standard adopted by Sensu, Icinga, and dozens of other tools.

Icinga was created in 2009 as a fork of Nagios by frustrated community contributors who felt the project was too closed. The name "Icinga" comes from a Zulu word meaning "it searches" or "it examines."
Datadog was founded in 2010 by Olivier Pomel and Alexis Le-Quoc. The name comes from a "DataDog" — a watchdog for your data. The company went public in 2019 with a market cap over $10 billion.

PagerDuty was founded in 2009 when actual pagers were already nearly extinct. The name deliberately evoked the old-school on-call experience. Co-founder Alex Solomon built the first version to replace a manual phone-tree escalation process.

Five nines (99.999%) availability means only 5.26 minutes of downtime per year. Each additional nine is exponentially harder to achieve. The concept was popularized by telecom companies in the 1990s, where Bell System targets predated modern SLOs.

The term "heartbeat" for health checks comes from the biological metaphor — a regular pulse that stops when the system is dead. Early cluster software like Heartbeat (Linux-HA, 1998) used the name literally.

Mean Time to Recovery (MTTR) and Mean Time to Failure (MTTF) come from reliability engineering in manufacturing, predating software by decades. Modern SRE teams focus more on MTTR because improving recovery speed is often easier than preventing all failures.

Google's SRE book distinguishes black-box monitoring (testing externally visible behavior) from white-box monitoring (using internal metrics). The terms were borrowed from software testing, where they date back to the 1960s.

Metric cardinality measures the number of unique time series. Adding a label with 1,000 values to a metric with 100 existing series creates 100,000 series. This exponential growth is the most common cause of monitoring system crashes.

Synthetic monitoring (running fake transactions to test a system) was pioneered by Keynote Systems in 1995. The term "canary" for early-warning tests comes from coal miners who used canary birds to detect toxic gases.
